Chapter 6: Ethical Dilemmas and the Weight of Compromise
There’s this moment—usually late at night—when the tough questions start creeping in. If you’ve ever worked in North Korea, you know what I mean. The line between right and wrong? It’s rarely clear. The rules you grew up with just don’t fit, and every decision seems to come with a hidden price tag.
It’s easy to look in from the outside and judge, but living inside that system means you’re constantly facing choices that never seem black and white.
Picture this: A foreign manager is approached by a local colleague. The request? Help getting medicine for his sick child. The medicine exists, but you can only get it through unofficial channels. If you help, you’re breaking the rules and risking trouble with the authorities. If you refuse, you’re turning your back on someone in real need.
In the end, the manager chooses to help—passing the medicine quietly, with just a word of caution. The father’s relief is immediate, so clear you can feel it. But for the manager, there’s still this nagging sense of unease, wondering if he’s really done the right thing.
These kinds of moments? They happen all the time. Every day brings a new ethical puzzle. Do you speak up about a safety issue, even if it might embarrass a local partner? Do you push for higher wages, knowing it could attract unwanted attention from officials?
Most people never have to make these kinds of choices. But in North Korea, compromise isn’t just common—it’s a way of life.
Then there’s the bigger question: Are you, as a foreigner, helping to support a repressive system just by being there? Or is it possible to make a real difference, even in small ways?
Honestly, there’s no easy answer. Some days, it feels like the work matters—creating jobs, sharing knowledge, building trust. Other days, the system feels so heavy, you wonder if it’s worth it, and the urge to just walk away is hard to ignore.
Let me share a moment. One evening, a foreigner sits with local friends, just sharing drinks and stories. The conversation drifts to dreams for the future. One friend, usually pretty quiet, suddenly says, “We want the same things you do. We want our kids to be safe, to have opportunities, to be happy.”
And in that instant, the lines between “us” and “them” start to blur. You’re reminded that, underneath it all, people are just people.
Living and working in North Korea means accepting that there are no simple answers. Every choice is a balancing act—a constant negotiation between your ideals and the reality around you.
If there’s one thing this experience teaches, it’s humility, empathy, and a real sense of the limits of good intentions.
